FINDING_ID: F001

SEVERITY: 0.86

FLAW_CLASS: 3

ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.42

FIND: Coherence pruning uses the wrong numerator, so pruning can increase the measured density rather than reduce it. Location: `_prune_for_coherence()` and downstream metric computation in `compose()` / `resolve_layer_conflicts()`. Evidence: the density is computed as `constraint_count / token_estimate`, where `constraint_count = _count_constraints(policy)`. That policy-derived count is not changed when SOFT packets or intra-packet SOFT directives are pruned. Pruning reduces `token_estimate` while leaving `constraint_count` constant, so `constraint_count / token_estimate` tends to rise, not fall. This contradicts the module contract: “constraint density … must stay below a per-model threshold. When exceeded, SOFT constraints are pruned.”

FOLLOW: Downstream consequences are material. `_prune_for_coherence()` can remove useful SOFT content while making the reported coherence density worse. `compose()` may then emit warnings even after exhausting all prunable content. The manifest reports misleading `constraint_count`, `constraint_density`, and `pruned_soft`, corrupting verification/accounting for prompt composition quality.

ANALYSE: HARD. Premises: mathematical density calculation and verification-integrity accounting are HARD constraints. Status: CONFIRMED by inspection. Falsification attempt: if pruning also reduced the numerator, the claim would fail; but the only numerator used in the shown pruning loop is `_count_constraints(policy)`, and no policy update occurs when packets are pruned. Residual-risk computation: `R_old=0.50`, `η=1.00`, `d=0.80`, `p=0.90`, so `q=0.7200`; `R_det=0.21875`; estimated `S_k=0.85`, `ν_b=0.03`, `ν_f=0.12`, `ν_eff=0.04746`; `R_base=0.26094`; `R_k=0.29601`. `S*=-1.835`, so the proposed fix is outside the valley of bad fixes. ADMISSIBILITY: `S_min=PASS`, `G-completeness=PASS`, `d_tool=PASS — direct symbolic inspection of update equation`, `σ_measured=N/A — patch not executed in repo`, `q_retest=PASS`. NOVELTY: `ν_k=0.00`, `c_ext=0.00 — no external search`, `H/H_max=0.42`, citations: none.

FIX:

<<<< SEARCH composer.py
def _count_constraints(policy: dict[str, Any]) -> int:

    count = 0

FINDING_ID: F002

SEVERITY: 0.88

FLAW_CLASS: 3

ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.51

FIND: HARD situation packets can be destructively transformed or silently truncated. Locations: the situation handling block in `compose()` and the global phenotype length cap after rendering. Evidence: `compose()` applies `_apply_phenotype_transform()` to every `situation` packet regardless of `constraint_class`. Some situation packets are explicitly HARD, e.g. `build_interaction_pattern("four_layer")`. `_apply_phenotype_transform()` can strip examples, strip rationales, simplify wording, compress tables, and truncate text. Later, the global cap slices `rendered` directly with `rendered[: transform.max_directive_chars]`, which can cut HARD content and leaves `packets`, `cid`, and manifest provenance describing untruncated content.

FOLLOW: This violates the documented invariant that HARD constraints are never pruned or weakened. It can also make `cid` and `manifest["packets"]` refer to packet text that is not actually present in `rendered_text`, causing unreproducible prompt attribution.

ANALYSE: HARD. Premises: explicit “HARD constraints are NEVER pruned” and provenance reproducibility are HARD verification-integrity constraints. Status: CONFIRMED. Falsification attempt: the claim would fail if the global cap only removed SOFT packets or raised on over-cap HARD content; the code instead performs raw string slicing after rendering. Residual-risk computation: `R_old=0.50`, `η=0.90`, `d=0.75`, `p=0.85`, so `q=0.57375`; `R_det=0.29886`; estimated `S_k=0.80`, `ν_b=0.04`, `ν_f=0.15`, `ν_eff=0.06880`; `R_base=0.33909`; `R_k=0.38456`. `S*=-0.7144`; proposed fix is acceptable. ADMISSIBILITY: `S_min=PASS`, `G-completeness=PASS`, `d_tool=PASS — branch/path inspection`, `σ_measured=N/A`, `q_retest=PASS`. NOVELTY: `ν_k=0.00`, `c_ext=0.00 — no external search`, `H/H_max=0.51`, citations: none.

FIX:

        packets.append(situation)
====

            packets.append(replace(situation))
        else:

FINDING_ID: F003

SEVERITY: 0.81

FLAW_CLASS: 4

ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.35

FIND: `_compute_cid()` does not hash directive content, so different directive sets can receive the same CID. Location: `_compute_cid()`. Evidence: the hash input is only `layer:name:len(text)` plus model. Two different packet texts with the same layer, name, length, and model collide deterministically even though the composed directive set is semantically different.

FOLLOW: CID is described as “composition identity hash” for attribution in analysis. A length-based hash can misattribute findings, merge different experimental prompts, and make reproduction impossible from CID alone. This is verification-integrity corruption in the provenance layer.

ANALYSE: HARD. Premises: reproducibility and provenance identity are HARD verification/accounting constraints. Status: CONFIRMED. Falsification attempt: if the CID included a digest of the packet text, the claim would fail; the current implementation includes only text length. Residual-risk computation: `R_old=0.50`, `η=1.00`, `d=0.70`, `p=0.80`, so `q=0.5600`; `R_det=0.30556`; estimated `S_k=0.75`, `ν_b=0.03`, `ν_f=0.12`, `ν_eff=0.05910`; `R_base=0.35417`; `R_k=0.39234`. `S*=-1.1478`; fix is acceptable. ADMISSIBILITY: `S_min=PASS`, `G-completeness=PASS`, `d_tool=PASS — deterministic collision argument`, `σ_measured=N/A`, `q_retest=PASS`. NOVELTY: `ν_k=0.00`, `c_ext=0.00 — no external search`, `H/H_max=0.35`, citations: none.

FIX:

```diff
<<<< SEARCH composer.py
def _compute_cid(packets: list[DirectivePacket], model: str) -> str:
    """Compute a deterministic composition identity hash."""
    components = [
        f"{p.layer}:{p.name}:{len(p.text)}" for p in packets
    ]
    components.append(f"model:{model}")
    raw = "|".join(components)
    return hashlib.sha256(raw.encode()).hexdigest()[:16]
====
def _compute_cid(packets: list[DirectivePacket], model: str) -> str:
    """Compute a deterministic composition identity hash."""
    components = [
        {
            "layer": p.layer,
            "name": p.name,
            "class": p.constraint_class,
            "domain": p.domain,
            "model": p.model,
            "tags": sorted(p.tags),
            "text_sha256": hashlib.sha256(p.text.encode()).hexdigest(),
        }
        for p in packets
    ]
    raw = json.dumps(
        {"model": model, "packets": components},
        sort_keys=True,
        separators=(",", ":"),
    )
    return hashlib.sha256(raw.encode()).hexdigest()[:16]
>>>> REPLACE
```

Alternative, dimension: mechanism. Differs from primary: instead of hashing full text digests, the CID could include the full rendered prompt hash once at the end of `compose()`. That is simpler but loses per-packet provenance granularity; the primary fix preserves both identity and packet-level attribution.

FINDING_ID: F004

SEVERITY: 0.74

FLAW_CLASS: 2

ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.28

FIND: `compose()` mutates caller-owned `DirectivePacket` objects passed as `situation`, contradicting the public API claim that composition is pure. Location: `compose()`, situation branch. Evidence: `situation.text = _apply_phenotype_transform(...)` mutates the same object supplied by the caller. If the caller reuses that packet for another model or another dispatch, the second composition receives already-transformed text rather than the original packet.

FOLLOW: This can cause cross-dispatch contamination. For example, composing once for a minimal model can strip or truncate the situation text; reusing the same packet for a full-context model then deprives that later model of content it should have received. This undermines determinism at the orchestration level even though a single call with identical current object state is deterministic.

ANALYSE: HARD. Premises: explicit public API contract says “Pure: no side effects, no state mutation.” Status: CONFIRMED by assignment to caller-owned object. Falsification attempt: if `compose()` used `replace()` or copied the packet before transformation, the claim would fail; the current code mutates directly. Residual-risk computation: `R_old=0.50`, `η=0.95`, `d=0.70`, `p=0.80`, so `q=0.5320`; `R_det=0.31880`; estimated `S_k=0.90`, `ν_b=0.02`, `ν_f=0.08`, `ν_eff=0.02784`; `R_base=0.33692`; `R_k=0.35538`. ADMISSIBILITY: `S_min=PASS`, `G-completeness=PASS`, `d_tool=PASS — state mutation path inspection`, `σ_measured=N/A`, `q_retest=PASS`. NOVELTY: `ν_k=0.00`, `c_ext=0.00 — no external search`, `H/H_max=0.28`, citations: none.

FIX:

This is fixed by the first SEARCH/REPLACE block in F002, which replaces direct mutation with `replace(...)` and also avoids destructive transforms for HARD situation packets:

```diff
<<<< SEARCH composer.py
    if situation:
        situation.text = _apply_phenotype_transform(situation.text, transform)
        packets.append(situation)
====
    if situation:
        if situation.constraint_class == "HARD":
            packets.append(replace(situation))
        else:
            packets.append(
                replace(
                    situation,
                    text=_apply_phenotype_transform(situation.text, transform),
                )
            )
>>>> REPLACE
```

Alternative, dimension: scope. Differs from primary: a narrower fix would simply call `situation = replace(situation)` before mutating `situation.text`. That would satisfy purity but would not address the separate HARD-packet weakening risk, so the broader F002/F004 shared fix is preferable.

---
